290.t: Social standing of musicians and his parents' reaction
290.s: Musicians were not scorned; his parents disliked practicing but approved later.
290.q: Oh, well, they, they used to put you, you know, I might say, on the shelf. Yeah. If you was, uh, you know, worthwhile talking about, you know, I'd say, use the word like worthwhile. Uh-huh. Talking about it, they put you, they, they say, you know, you was good, you was alright, you was a good…

717.t: Parents' reaction to a musical career
717.s: His parents liked the piano but panicked as he got serious and went on the road young, then calmed down.
717.q: That’s funny. Well they liked the fact that I was playing the piano you know, but when I really started to get serious about it they got a little panicky. Because my father would play gigs, get home at four in the morning and open up the barber shop at six. So of course my mother said look, it’s…

741.t: His parents and not finishing Berklee
741.s: His parents never fully understood his career or accepted that he left Berklee without a degree.
741.ch: Johnny Hammond, Dreams and moving to New York
741.q: Eventually they did but it took a long time I think. I don’t know if it ever really quite sunk in, you know, because they’d always say well why don’t you — can’t you go back — because I didn’t quite finish Berklee. I didn’t get the degree, the music ed degree. And they said, “Can’t you go back to…

485.t: Father's reaction to dance hall work
485.s: Her father disapproved of a daughter playing in dance halls, but good pay and her mother's support won him over.
485.ch: Dance halls and learning jazz in Japan
485.q: Well firstly he was very, very upset because in the Japanese, traditionally middle class family on, daughters are not supposed to work. They marry someone. And on top of that playing in dance halls, my God, that’s an evil place. But I was paid tremendous money in those days. And it was very helpful…

510.t: His mother's reaction to his career change
510.s: His mother wanted him to be a doctor and was upset he quit; she liked that he played with Miles Davis and Lou Rawls more than the music itself.
510.ch: Early life and path to music
510.q: Hell. That’s the only thing, for want of a better word. Take into consideration the time. It was the sixties, the fifties and sixties. I’m a black American growing up in a certain kind of environment and the revolution wasn’t really going on when I was going to school, I’m talking about ’58, ’59.…

1032.t: Young Cuban women musicians, their parents and Cuba's love of music
1032.s: Parents were generally supportive; everyone in Cuba has opinions about music. She first went around 1981-82.
1032.q: No, not at all. I just hoped that their parents wouldn’t get in the way and try and stop it, but generally, you know Cubans love music and you know it’s so deep in peoples’ lives. That that’s one of the things I’ve loved so much about Cuba is everybody loves music. And if you’re a musician they…

436.t: Pete's father wanted his sons to be musicians; joining the union at 13
436.s: Pete reflects on his father steering him and Conte away from factory work toward music, and joining the South Bend union at 13.
436.q: I don’t have, oddly enough I don’t even have the old “Peter Gunn” things with Hank Mancini. That was twenty, forty, thirty years ago, something like that.

206.s: His parents wanted a farmer and a minister; he got over homesickness and roomed with Gozzo.
206.q: They didn’t envision me as a traveling musician that’s for sure. They wanted me to be a farmer. And my brother Art they wanted to be a Methodist minister. And we failed them.

325.t: Parents, the family store and the start-up loan
325.s: His parents wanted a doctor or lawyer but ran a small retail store; his father gave him a lump sum to start a business.
325.ch: Teenage obsession and the record store
325.q: I wouldn’t have had much of an answer for them. I didn’t know what my future was going to be and in fact my parents hoped, you know, I would become a doctor or a lawyer and all of those things. But they had no clue how to orient themselves to guiding me in that direction. My dad owned a small…

209.t: Parents' reaction and the Chuck Cabot band, 1944
209.s: His parents were supportive but worried; his mother found six white shirts for his first road job with Chuck Cabot, a high school coach whose brother was Johnny Richards.
209.ch: First road band and learning jazz
209.q: They were supportive. They were concerned the first time I went on the road at 16, and my father gave me a talk about girls. And the war was still on then, because this was in 1944. And things were in short supply, certain things. And one of them were white dress shirts. And I needed them for this,…

336.t: Leaving at 18 with Carmen Cavallaro; parents' reaction
336.s: He took the Cavallaro gig at 18; supportive blue-collar parents warned about the insecurity of music.
336.q: Well they were very supportive. They were blue collar people. They tried to warn me of the pitfalls and they were right. They said that’s a pretty rough way to make a living. You know, what are you going to do when there’s no work, and so forth, and job security and so forth. And I said I don’t…

502.t: His parents' reaction to a music career
502.s: His mother was worried and his father suggested a trade, but he feels fortunate to have always had just enough.
502.q: I think so. I think that she was worried, you know, and my father always said, “Well why don’t you just like be a barber or something, have a trade.” And he was probably right, because it with the oscilloscope pattern of the ups and downs of music, I probably should have had a trade or something.…

749.t: Her mother's support and her father's objection to music school
749.s: Her mother, not her father, encouraged her to go to the University of Miami.
749.q: No. Not at all. My father did. It was my father, not my mother. It is my mother who’s responsible for this beautiful experience I had in life and having seen the world. And without her encouragement and without her creating and finding every possible way to make this happen I wouldn’t be talking to…

341.t: Her mother and the first Broadway sub job
341.s: Her mother came to accept her career; she remembers her mother waving from the fourth row when she subbed in the Cabaret revival.
341.ch: Growing up in Endicott and learning drums
341.q: I think when she — she didn’t come to all the high school performances but some of them, and I think — I won’t say when I started to make money, but when she heard people clapping. She’s like oh that’s my daughter. And like the funniest thing was in New York when I got to sub in my first Broadway…

104.t: Leaving school for Billy Mayall's four-piano act and her parents' reaction
104.s: She joined a vaudeville act, her father offered money to stop her, and a cousin was appalled at the Hickory House.
104.q: Oh, God. Well I didn’t really know I was going to do that. I had gone to this piano player, Billy Mayall, thinking he would give me a few pointers about jazz. And I mean I was so stupid, he wasn’t really a jazz player so much as a popular player, but of course he did play good chords and good…

586.t: Gradual switch to bass and her mother's support
586.s: She moved to bass gradually, decided to focus on it by senior year, and her mother supported and drove her everywhere.
586.ch: Taking up bass and high school
586.q: Oh yes well because I had — well I didn’t actually just switch, you know. I didn’t say I’m playing guitar today and tomorrow I’m playing bass. It was gradual. So I just kind of played bass on the side. I also played, when I was in high school, a year I did bassoon, I played baritone horn in the…

487.t: Parents' reaction and his mother at the Village Gate
487.s: Parents wanted a profession; he decided on music after summer 1958; his mother cheered at a Mongo Santamaria show.
487.ch: Growing up and discovering Latin music
487.q: Not at all. Not at all. I was — after high school I was accepted to Columbia College, and they were looking for some kind of profession, preferably a lawyer, something like that. And after my first summer at Columbia, which was the summer of ’58, it was like an epiphany. I said boy this is what…

531.s: Her parents supported music but had trepidations once she wanted jazz saxophone as a living.
531.q: They were until I said this is what I want to do for a living. Then they did have their trepidations. They let me go ahead and they became more and more supportive. They were supportive of me playing music always because everybody in the family loved music. But jazz and saxophone — that was quite a…

396.t: Her father's horror at a daughter in jazz, and Smith College
396.s: Her father and brother Richard played music; her father, who had saved for Smith College, was appalled that she wanted jazz, recalling how musicians treated women on cruises.
396.q: Yes. And that’s what I heard since I was quite young. I heard my father playing along with his records ever since I was born, and also practicing the various etudes and concertos and stuff.

222.t: His mother's feelings about a music career
222.s: She doubted it until he joined the union at 16 and showed he could earn money.
222.q: At first she didn’t like it. She didn’t think that I would really get into it anyhow. She figured well he’ll probably change his mind and decide to go into something else like become a doctor, a school teacher or something. But the fact that I started out during World War II, or the latter part of…

225.t: Parents' reluctance about touring with Snookum Russell
225.s: His father opposed his leaving home but his mother persuaded him to come around.
225.q: this enterprise. My mother took the stance that, well, we may as well support him in this because he’s going to do it anyway. Since we can’t stop him, we may as well go along with the program and endorse it. Finally my dad came around and said, "Well, yeah. You’re right."

508.t: Choosing music over acting; his father lets him lose six hundred dollars
508.s: He decided against a Hollywood career on his own; his father recalled letting him cash a bad check as a lesson.
508.ch: Radio, acting and playing outside jazz
508.q: Who could you talk to really? Who could you talk to? So many people want to be movie stars. They’ll say like, “Man, you gotta go for this. This is your opportunity.” You know, I’m going to make my own decisions. My parents want it like that. This is what I think you should do, but you need to do….…

114.t: His family's support for becoming a musician
114.s: His family supported his musical ambitions, and he says he never thought about money.
114.q: Of course, yeah. My mother -- yeah. Because that's what I wanted to do. And I think it -- I think any family. You know what I think is wrong is for a person to say, "I want you to make some money, so I want you to be a doctor." You know, no. The kid wants to be a doctor,

117.t: Father and the Ray Noble band film foot
117.s: Freeman's father first saw him in a film with the Ray Noble band, recognizing only his foot; Freeman promises the Noble story later.
117.q: Now, my dad was not to see me do anything or hear me do anything until I joined the Ray Noble band. You remember the story of the Ray Noble band.
